newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SMITHKLINE CHALLENGES S.AFRICAN DRUG REFORMS.
newsitem.headline: SMITHKLINE CHALLENGES S.AFRICAN DRUG REFORMS.

text.p: Anglo-American drugs giant SmithKline Beecham Plc is taking legal action to overturn South African government moves which would make prescribing generic drugs mandatory and limit the dispensing of medicines.

SmithKline has filed a submission asking the Supreme Court's Transvaal Division to overturn health minister Nkosazana Zuma's proposed regulation, called R1150, part of an overall reform programme for healthcare in South Africa.
SmithKline South Africa chief executive Gunter Faber declined to comment on the move. "We have no comment to make," he said on Friday.
However, a company source confirmed the group had filed the submission.

Generic drugs are off-patent versions of branded products and are usually much cheaper. But the industry says moves to limit the use of branded drugs denies doctors choice and could force them to change established patient regimens.
The pharmaceutical industry puts great store on its money-spinning branded drugs and firms fiercely defend their patents from all challengers.

Zuma also plans to allow only, as yet undefined, licensed persons to be able to dispense medicine. The industry fears that may rule out many currently dispensing medical practitioners, such as dentists.
The source said SmithKline had the full support of other companies in South Africa and said it was prepared to fight the proposed plans through the courts.
"We have the backing of other companies, not only multi-nationals, but local ones too," the source said.

The already disastrous relationship between Zuma and the drugs industry has been further soured by claims international firms have been threatened with expulsion from South Africa if the legal challenge goes ahead.
Mirryena Deeb, chief executive of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association, said reports of threats to international firms had been recieved by the organisation.
"My office has received complaints of threats to multi-national firms. They (the complaints) have come from head offices abroad. It is a great concern to us," she said.
The Smithkline source said it had received an alleged threat: "That did happen. But I don't think it came from the minister (Zuma), but from someone else in the ministry."
No-one at the Health Ministry was immediately available for comment, but the Financial Mail newspaper quoted spokesman Vincent Hlongwane denying any threats had been made.

This latest dispute comes after a blazing row earlier this month when President Nelson Mandela made a veiled reference to multi-national drug firms playing a role in the scandal over funding for the Sarafina 2 AIDS awareness play. That scandal has prompted calls for Zuma to resign.
The drugs industry has denied the accusations.
Deeb said the latest dispute came at a critical time for the industry with many multi-national firms considering whether to replace or upgrade ageing South African facilities.
Such new investment is vital to South Africa, but is now under threat, she said. "They are very upset and they are concerned about it. They are here to invest and they want certainty," she added.
Earlier this month the South African arm of German drugs group Boehringer Mannheim warned foreign firms may pull out of the country if they are made to feel unwelcome.
"If an industry is not welcome in a country, then companies have to think about down-sizing of operations and moving into a more friendly environment," said chief executive Knut Seifert.
